A patient with severe liver disease is asked to hold their arms outstretched with wrists extended. Their hands repeatedly flap downwards.

What is this sign called?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Ataxia is impaired coordination of movement, not a flapping tremor. C. Fasciculations are fine spontaneous twitches of muscle fibres seen in lower motor neurone disease. D. Dysdiadochokinesia is impaired rapid alternating movement, a sign of cerebellar dysfunction. E. Chorea consists of irregular, flowing involuntary movements, not a rhythmic flap of outstretched hands.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Asterixis is a flapping tremor of outstretched, extended hands caused by negative myoclonus; it occurs in hepatic encephalopathy, CO2 retention and uraemia.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Severe liver disease ↓ Arms outstretched, wrists extended ↓ Hands repeatedly flap down ↓ Brief lapses of postural tone ↓ B, asterixis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, chorea — tempting as an involuntary movement disorder, but chorea is irregular and flowing, not a repetitive flap of outstretched hands.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Flapping tremor in liver disease is asterixis: think hepatic encephalopathy.

options.A: Fresh blood passed with the urine on voiding

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vomited blood is haematemesis; coughed-up blood is haemoptysis.

An older adult develops unexplained new-onset diabetes together with weight loss.

Why might pancreatic disease be considered?

options.A: Chronic pancreatitis is the commonest cause of diabetes in older adults

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Ten-plus days of purulent discharge and facial pain — think bacterial sinusitis.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with advanced cancer has severe breathlessness despite treatment of the underlying disease.

What is an important principle of palliative care?

options.A: Manage symptoms alongside the underlying disease and the patient's goals
options.B: Defer palliative care referral until the last days of life
options.C: Escalate disease-directed treatment before addressing symptoms
options.D: Stop all active treatment once palliative care is involved
options.E: Avoid discussing prognosis to protect the patient from distress

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Manage symptoms alongside the underlying disease and the patient's goals
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Palliative care focuses on relieving distressing symptoms, such as breathlessness, alongside disease-directed treatment where appropriate, guided by the patient's priorities and goals of care.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Palliative care can be provided early in a serious illness, not only at the end of life. C. Symptoms should be managed alongside treatment, with treatments reviewed for benefit and burden. D. Palliative care can be delivered alongside appropriate active treatment. E. Honest, sensitive communication about prognosis is central to palliative care.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Palliative care is not only for the last days of life: it can run alongside disease-directed treatment, focusing on symptoms such as breathlessness and on what matters most to the patient.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Advanced cancer with severe breathlessness ↓ underlying disease already treated ↓ symptom still distressing ↓ palliative care addresses symptoms at any stage ↓ manage symptoms alongside disease and the patient's goals
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, stop all active treatment once palliative care is involved — tempting because palliative care is linked with end of life, but it can be delivered alongside appropriate active treatment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Palliative care runs alongside treatment, guided by symptoms and the patient's goals.

options.A: Daily phosphate enemas as first-line treatment
options.B: Urgent colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer
options.C: Increase fibre, fluids and physical activity
options.D: Prescribe loperamide to help regulate her stools
options.E: Switch to a low-fibre, low-residue diet for 4 weeks

live_plab_copy.pearl: Uncomplicated chronic constipation: start with fibre, fluids and activity, then a bulk-forming laxative, then an osmotic laxative such as a macrogol if needed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Infrequent hard stools with straining ↓ chronic course ↓ no alarm symptoms ↓ increase fibre, fluids and physical activity
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, Urgent colonoscopy — cancer worries make it tempting, but without alarm features investigation is not needed; lifestyle measures come first.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Constipation without red flags: lifestyle first, then laxatives stepwise.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Accurate BP: right cuff, bare arm at heart level, rested patient.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with longstanding inflammatory disease has anaemia. Which pattern is most consistent with anaemia of chronic disease?

options.A: Macrocytosis caused by vitamin B12 deficiency
options.B: Low ferritin with severe iron depletion
options.D: Low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Inflammation increases hepcidin, reducing circulating iron while iron stores are often preserved or increased.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 deficiency is a separate cause of macrocytic anaemia. B. Low ferritin is characteristic of iron deficiency. C. Anaemia means haemoglobin is reduced. E. Increased B12 does not explain the typical pattern.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammation raises hepcidin, trapping iron in stores; serum iron is low but ferritin is normal or high, unlike iron deficiency.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Longstanding inflammatory disease ↓ Inflammation raises hepcidin ↓ Iron trapped in stores ↓ Serum iron falls, stores preserved ↓ Low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, low ferritin with severe iron depletion — both share low serum iron, but low ferritin means absent stores, which defines iron deficiency.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Low iron with normal or high ferritin suggests anaemia of chronic disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor and a sore tongue. Blood tests show macrocytosis and a low vitamin B12 level. Which neurological symptom can occur with vitamin B12 deficiency?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy, producing paraesthesia, numbness and impaired proprioception.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Seizures are not a characteristic neurological manifestation of B12 deficiency. B. Sudden monocular blindness suggests an ocular vascular emergency. C. A resting tremor is classically associated with Parkinson disease. E. Facial weakness suggests a facial nerve disorder.
live_plab_copy.pearl: B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord; neurological damage can occur and may become irreversible without prompt replacement.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Fatigue and sore tongue ↓ Macrocytosis ↓ Low vitamin B12 ↓ B12 is needed for myelin ↓ Peripheral paraesthesia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, resting tremor — it is a neurological sign, but it is classically parkinsonian and not a feature of B12 deficiency.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: B12 deficiency can cause paraesthesia and proprioceptive loss: replace it promptly.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anaemia. Reticulocyte count is very low.

Which infection is classically associated with this presentation?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Parvovirus B19 temporarily suppresses erythropoiesis and can cause an aplastic crisis in people with chronic haemolytic anaemia such as sickle cell disease.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis. C. Varicella-zoster causes chickenpox and shingles. D. Rhinovirus commonly causes the common cold. E. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Parvovirus B19 briefly halts red-cell production; in chronic haemolysis this causes a sudden aplastic crisis with a very low reticulocyte count, which may need transfusion.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sickle cell disease ↓ Sudden severe anaemia ↓ Very low reticulocytes = marrow not responding ↓ Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, Epstein–Barr virus — a familiar childhood viral infection with blood changes, but it causes infectious mononucleosis, not selective red-cell aplasia in haemolytic anaemia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sickle cell plus sudden anaemia plus low reticulocytes = parvovirus B19.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient has a macrocytic anaemia. Which additional feature would point to vitamin B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological disease (peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord, with loss of vibration and proprioception), whereas folate deficiency does not typically cause this neurological syndrome.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Macrocytosis occurs in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it does not discriminate. B. Mildly raised bilirubin from ineffective erythropoiesis occurs with either deficiency. C. Both deficiencies cause megaloblastic anaemia. D. Fatigue is a non-specific feature of anaemia from either cause.
live_plab_copy.pearl: B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord; never give folic acid alone in megaloblastic anaemia until B12 deficiency is excluded or treated.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Macrocytic anaemia ↓ B12 and folate deficiency share the blood picture ↓ Only B12 deficiency damages myelin ↓ Neurological symptoms point to B12
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, raised serum bilirubin — tempting as a sign of ineffective erythropoiesis, but it occurs in folate deficiency too and does not discriminate.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Macrocytosis plus neurological signs = B12; replace B12 before folate.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 72-year-old man has iron-deficiency anaemia without an obvious dietary explanation. What should be considered particularly important in the investigation of an older adult?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult requires assessment for potential gastrointestinal blood loss, including malignancy.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis without iron deficiency. C. Anaemia of chronic kidney disease is a different pattern and does not explain true iron deficiency. D. Autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) can impair iron absorption, but in an older adult gastrointestinal blood loss, including malignancy, must be excluded first. E. Sideroblastic anaemia is a disorder of iron utilisation rather than iron deficiency.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult needs upper and lower GI investigation for occult blood loss, including gastric and colorectal cancer, plus coeliac serology.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ No dietary explanation ↓ Older adult, so occult malignancy is a real risk ↓ Look for gastrointestinal blood loss
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, pernicious anaemia — autoimmune gastritis can impair iron absorption, but GI blood loss, including cancer, is the priority to exclude in an older adult.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult: investigate the GI tract.

A patient has macrocytic anaemia but no neurological symptoms. Their diet is poor and they drink substantial amounts of alcohol.

Which deficiency is a possible cause?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia and is associated with poor diet and alcohol excess.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency causes a bleeding tendency. B. Iron deficiency is usually microcytic. C. Vitamin D deficiency affects bone and calcium metabolism. E. Vitamin C deficiency causes connective-tissue and bleeding manifestations.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia without neuropathy; poor diet and alcohol excess are classic causes. Check B12 too before replacing folate.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, iron deficiency — the commonest nutritional anaemia, but it usually causes a microcytic picture, not macrocytosis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Macrocytosis with poor diet and alcohol, no neuropathy: think folate.
